title: The Adventures of Pinocchio
author: Carlo Collodi
openingText: “Once upon a time…” “There was a king!” my young readers will say at once. “No, children, you’ve got it wrong. Once upon a time there was a piece of wood.” It was not fine, expensive wood, but an ordinary piece from a woodpile, the kind people put in stoves and fireplaces in winter to light a fire and warm their rooms. I don’t know how it happened, but the fact is that one day this piece of wood ended up in the workshop of an old carpenter whose name was Master Antonio, though everyone called him Master Cherry, because the tip of his nose was always shiny and dark red, like a ripe cherry.
about:
The Adventures of Pinocchio opens in the workshop of a carpenter called Master Cherry, who is about to turn a log into a table leg when the log cries out. He gives it to his poor neighbour Geppetto, who carves it into a puppet and names him Pinocchio. The puppet runs away before he has learned to walk properly, and the rest of the book follows him from one adventure to the next: a puppet theatre, an inn, a pair of swindlers called the Fox and the Cat, a field where coins are said to grow, prison, a farmer's chain, an island, the Land of Toys, and the belly of an enormous Shark.

All along he keeps resolving to be good, to go to school and to go home to Geppetto, and keeps being led off again. A Talking Cricket warns him, a Fairy with blue hair rescues him and gives him second chances, and his nose grows when he lies. The book is comic, quick and sometimes dark, and it ends with Pinocchio caring for his father and becoming a real boy.

Carlo Lorenzini, who wrote as Collodi, published the story in weekly instalments in a Roman magazine from July 1881. He first ended it after fifteen chapters and then continued it at his editor's request; the complete book was published in Florence in 1883. Tinct's English and Danish editions are translated directly from the Italian text of the 1902 Bemporad edition.

angleCards.title: Promises and detours.
angleCards.text: Almost every chapter turns on the same moment: Pinocchio has promised to do one thing, and something more tempting appears on the road. Following those moments shows how the book is built and why each detour costs more than the last.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track each promise Pinocchio makes, what tempts him away from it, and what it costs him.

angleCards.title: A hard world.
angleCards.text: Collodi's Tuscany is poor. Geppetto has no food in the house, the judge jails the victim, and animals and people alike are bought and sold. The comedy plays out against hunger and injustice, and the book does not pretend otherwise.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to notice how hunger, money and injustice shape what happens to Pinocchio and the people around him.

angleCards.title: The Fairy and the Cricket.
angleCards.text: Two voices keep telling Pinocchio the truth: a cricket he flattens with a hammer in chapter four, and a Fairy who forgives him again and again. Watching how he answers them, and how they answer him, follows the book's moral line.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the Talking Cricket and the Fairy with the blue hair, and how Pinocchio's answers to them change.

angleCards.title: From puppet to boy.
angleCards.text: The ending turns on what Pinocchio does, not on a spell. Reading toward the last chapters, ask what has really changed in him, and what the book thinks a real boy is.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read for what changes in Pinocchio, and what the book treats as the difference between a puppet and a boy.

cast.name: Pinocchio
cast.description: A wooden puppet carved from a talking log. He is quick, cheeky, kind-hearted and endlessly easy to talk into things. He means every promise he makes and breaks most of them, and when he lies, his nose grows.

cast.name: Geppetto
cast.description: A poor old man with a yellow wig, called Polendina by the neighbourhood boys, which makes him furious. He carves the puppet to earn a living with him, calls him his son, and gives up his breakfast and his coat for him.

cast.name: The Fairy with the blue hair
cast.description: First seen as a pale girl at the window of a house in the woods, she takes the puppet in, calls doctors to his bed and forgives him again and again. She appears in different forms through the book, always firm and always ready to give him another chance.

cast.name: The Talking Cricket
cast.description: A cricket who has lived in Geppetto's room for more than a hundred years and tells Pinocchio plainly where disobedience leads. The puppet does not want to hear it, but the Cricket turns up again later in the book.

cast.name: The Fox and the Cat
cast.description: A lame fox and a blind cat who are neither lame nor blind. They flatter Pinocchio, eat his dinner at his expense, and talk him into planting his gold coins in the Field of Miracles.

cast.name: Candlewick
cast.description: A thin, lazy schoolmate whose real name is Romeo and whom everyone calls Candlewick. He is the boy Pinocchio likes best, and he has a plan to leave for a country where there is no school and every day is a holiday.

whyItMatters.title: A puppet with a will of his own
whyItMatters.body: Pinocchio is not a model. He is greedy, vain, impulsive and gullible, and also generous, quick to cry and quick to love. Collodi does not lecture him into goodness; he lets the puppet learn from consequences, some of them very hard, and from the people who keep caring for him anyway. That mixture is why the character has lasted: he is recognisable, and his failures are funny before they are serious.

whyItMatters.title: Comedy with an edge
whyItMatters.body: Much of the book is slapstick and wordplay: a carpenter and a woodcarver wrestling over a wig, a judge who is a gorilla, a town called Foolcatcher whose streets are full of the fleeced and the plucked. Beneath it lies a sharp picture of a poor, unfair society, written by a satirical journalist who had seen a good deal of it. The laughter and the hardship belong together.

whyItMatters.title: A story many people know only secondhand
whyItMatters.body: Pinocchio has been retold, filmed and softened many times. Collodi's own book is stranger and more surprising than most versions: the Cricket's fate in chapter four, the hanging at the Great Oak, the donkeys at the circus. Reading the original shows how much the familiar story has left out.
